newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: DEL MONTE RESHAPES IN EUROPE, EYES PARTNERS.
newsitem.headline: DEL MONTE RESHAPES IN EUROPE, EYES PARTNERS.

text.p: South Africa's Del Monte Royal Foods Ltd on Wednesday tried to shake off a disastrous trading period by staking its future on a massive European shake-up and casting into new markets for alliances.
Earlier the firm, battered by internal problems and a tough trading environment, posted a drop in first half attributable profit to 40.09 million rand from 60.82 million.

The firm's restructuring, centred in Europe, will cost 360 million rand. The firm also said that due to the trading performance of its business it had elected to write down the value of its trademarks and brands by 1.2 billion rand.
Del Monte said it expected to reap the full benefits of the restructuring by the third year of its implementation and the benefits are estimated at a 100 million rand per year.
Europe has been the main source of the firm's woes with a profit collapse in Italy after a mismanaged acquisition and also a strong battering at the hands of a resurgent pound sterling.
In Europe all currencies except the Greek drachma moved against the firm's operations.

New Del Monte Europe president Francois de Lavalette said the European operation would now concentrate on its core canned fruit and pineapple businesses and take strong action to cut costs, particularly in Italy. "The difficulties of Italy have proven to be bigger and deeper than we we expected," he said.

The firm is to sell-off some non-core Italian assets in a move it hopes will cover about 80 percent of the 198 million rand cash cost of the restructuring. De Lavalette said the firm had already attracted some very interested buyers.

De Lavalette said Del Monte was committed to its European fruit juice business, but they were not considered core units. "Pineapples are the heart of our business...our position in juice is important, but not part of our core business," he said.

Del Monte would seek to drive down the costs of its branded products in order to meet the threat from own-label rivals that are especially common in Europe. "If we want to compete with own-labels we must at least get our own costs down to own-label companies," he added.
The group is also pinning hopes on securing a network of new alliances and joint-ventures across Europe and into new markets.

The firm has recently moved for the first time into Russia with a joint-venture and Turkey with a licensing agreement. De Lavalette said it was hoped these moves would form the blue-print for expansion into Eastern and Central Europe.
"This is going to one of the most crucial long-term movements the company has to make in order to succeed," he said.
Del Monte is also in talks with several possible partners in Britain aimed at securing an alliance that would reduce the costs of its juice operations there.
One shining piece of good news for the firm has been the strong performance of its Phillipine operation which saw profits rise to 34 million rand in the first half from 24 million rand.

The operation is buoyed by a strong local markets, improved agricultural practises that have boosted pineapple yields and low costs. "The Phillipines remain by far our strongest partner," said Del Monte chairman Vivian Imerman.
Imerman added that the unit had expanded with an Indian joint-venture and was hoping to use that as a launchpad to move the Del Monte brand into other Asian markets.
